# Open Questions {#sec-open}

A reading gets to live in a chapter when a manual, the source, or a probe
supports it. These are the ones that do not clear that bar yet. They are
recorded so the chapters do not quietly upgrade them into mechanisms.

## The symbol `gp` bits

Inspect lines for symbols in the original session carried `gp` values such
as `0x4000`, `0x5000`, `0x6000`, `0x7000`, and `0x8000`, often next to
`LCK` and "(has value)". `CHARSXP` lines carried smaller values such as
`0x60` and `0x61`, and inspect already translated the part a human needs
(`ASCII`, `cached`). The general-purpose field is sixteen bits whose
meaning depends on the type. The
[CHARSXP encoding section](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html#Encodings-for-CHARSXPs)
covers one dialect. The symbol dialect lives in the source, and this book
does not publish a decoded table it has not checked bit by bit against
that source.

What would close it: a short comment in `src/main/inspect.c` or the symbol
macros in the headers, quoted next to one fresh dump, for the current R.

## Does inspect suppress `REF(0)`?

Empty vectors in the session printed an empty bracket. Saturated and
shared nodes printed `REF(n)`. The reading in @sec-header is that a
missing token means "nothing worth printing," not "this node has no count
field." The field exists either way: under the reference-counting build
it is the 16-bit `named` slot.

What would close it: the `Rprintf` in `do_inspect` that emits `REF(%d)`.
If it is guarded by a non-zero test, the reading becomes a mechanism. Until
then, do not write code that infers a zero count from the absence of the
token.

## The sixth name on an `S7_property`

A property built as `class_any` inspected as a length-6 record. The paste
showed `name`, `class`, `getter`, `setter`, and `validator`, and elided
the last name. @sec-types refuses to guess it. The argument does not
depend on the sixth name. The five that are visible already include the
slots a strict property would fill.

What would close it: `S7:::prop_names()` or the constructor in the S7
sources for the installed version, plus one inspect that does not elide.

## Does S7 pin the class at `REFCNTMAX`?

Before the replacement, the class closure in the session had a finite
`REF`. Inside the instance dump after `@p <-`, the class node appeared
saturated. That can happen because many holders exist (the instance, the
binding, the IDE, internal caches) or because something called
`MARK_NOT_MUTABLE`. Saturation is a one-way door in the macros: once the
count hits the ceiling, decrement will not bring it back. Treating "S7
classes are immortal" as a mechanism would be an overread of one dump.

What would close it: a quiet session, `lobstr::ref` on the class before
and after instantiation, and a look at whether S7 sets the count on
purpose.

## Base-level constructors for weak references

The session reached for `rlang::new_weakref` and got a real `WEAKREFSXP`.
`reg.finalizer` is base. A user-facing weak-map constructor in base, of
the same shape as rlang's, was not part of the session and is not claimed
here. The distinction between "the runtime has the type" and "the standard
library hands it to you" is the point of that section. A future base
function would narrow the gap without changing the type.

## `1:n` and ALTREP, on this R

The design of ALTREP is documented. The session that seeded this book did
not paste `inspect(1:1e9)`. Whether a given R build still represents that
sequence compactly, and how inspect spells the ALTREP class name, is a
probe worth running and not a fact this text pretends to have run.

## User databases

[R Internals on environments](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html#Environments-and-variable-lookup)
still mentions "user databases" and points, a bit sheepishly, at the
former Omegahat package `RObjectTables`. The manual calls the hook
under-documented. Treat it as archaeology until you have a current C
caller. It is not a third environment model you should design a package
around.

## Two PowerShell docs, one introduction date

[about_Output_Streams](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_output_streams)
and
[about_Redirection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_redirection)
agree on the stream numbers and disagree, in places, about which
PowerShell version introduced warning, verbose, and debug as redirectable
streams. This book uses the numbers and the roles, which agree, and does
not adjudicate the version history.

## What would change a recommendation

The container split (value for facts, handle for capabilities) would
weaken if ordinary S7 replacement stopped changing object identity, or if
environments grew copy-on-modify of their bindings. Neither is likely.
The recommendation to fill S7 property slots instead of checking in
methods would weaken if property validators stopped running on
replacement. The S7 design notes keep a ledger of that kind of
version-sensitive mechanic; defer to it for S7 behavior, and re-check
after a major S7 release.

The recommendation to prefer calling handlers over `tryCatch` would not
survive a problem whose correct policy is always "this attempt is over."
It is a default, not a law. The law is that the choice should be made on
purpose, in one place, with a class a caller can see.
